segments.title: Reference books for Blackburn aircraft
segments.summary: A British aircraft-specification reference and A. J. Jackson's Blackburn Aircraft since 1909 provide two starting points for tracing the company's designs.
segments.body: The sources shown are a British aircraft-specification reference and A. J. Jackson's Blackburn Aircraft since 1909. The copy of Jackson's book once belonged to Aberdeenshire Library and Information Services, and Putnam published it in 1968. One source organizes aircraft around their specifications, while the other follows Blackburn's designs over time. Using both makes it easier to trace an individual aircraft and compare it with the manufacturer's wider work.

segments.title: Why Blackburn's period aircraft names need checking
segments.summary: A history website helps reconcile older Blackburn aircraft names and variant labels with the names used by modern institutions.
segments.body: The British Aerospace history website can help when a period aircraft name does not match the label used by a modern institution. Names used in the 1920s and 1930s sometimes differ from today's dominant terminology, and a label once attached to a variant may later become the best-known name for the whole aircraft. The preference for period names came from doctoral research on aircraft carriers and naval aviation in those decades. That work examined how carriers and aircraft developed alongside each other, making consistent identification necessary when following their connected histories. The passage offers a concise lesson in source criticism: check period usage, variant names, and later terminology before assuming two labels describe different designs.

evidence.note: The transcript recommends a British Aerospace history site and explains the mismatch between period aircraft names, variants, and later naming.
